input: It is a familiar observation in the study of transport processes that momentum, heat, and mass transfer are closely analogous to one another, since all three are brought about by essentially the same fluid motion within the fluid layer. This idea is taken a good deal further by the Chilton-Colburn analogy, which expresses the analogy in the form of a definite working relationship between the mass-transfer factor $j_D$ and the friction factor $f$, namely the relationship $j_D = f/2$, which holds good in those cases where the friction at the surface is due to skin friction alone. The practical value of this result is considerable, because it means that the mass-transfer factor can be obtained directly from a friction measurement, without the need for a separate mass-transfer experiment. By way of a short numerical illustration, if the friction factor $f$ has the value 0.0064, then the analogy gives the mass-transfer factor $j_D$ as 0.0032, so that the one quantity is read off from the other in a very straightforward way. It must be emphasised, however, that the analogy breaks down in cases where the pressure drop is produced by form drag rather than by skin friction. In the flow across a tube bank, for example, the fluid separates from the surface of each tube, and a part of the pressure drop is expended in maintaining the wake behind the tube; this contribution to the friction factor has no counterpart in mass transfer, and the value of the mass-transfer factor deduced from the friction factor will consequently be too high
target: The three transfer processes are treated together because the same fluid motion moves momentum, heat and mass through a fluid layer, and the comparison is more than a resemblance of form. The Chilton-Colburn analogy turns the comparison into a working relation between the mass-transfer factor $j_D$ and the friction factor $f$: where the friction on a surface comes from skin friction alone, the analogy sets the two equal in the form $j_D = f/2$. A friction measurement then yields the mass-transfer factor directly, with no separate mass-transfer experiment. A short check shows the size of the step the analogy takes: for a friction factor $f$ of 0.0064, the relation gives a mass-transfer factor $j_D$ of 0.0032, read off the friction factor with no further data. The check is short because the analogy leaves nothing else to determine: one measured factor supplies the other in full. The analogy fails where the pressure drop is produced by form drag rather than by skin friction. In flow across a tube bank the fluid separates from the surface of each tube, and part of the pressure drop pays for the wake behind the tube; that part of the friction factor has no counterpart in mass transfer, because the separated wake does not transfer mass in the way the attached layer does. The friction factor then counts drag the analogy cannot use, and a mass-transfer factor taken from it comes out too high, by the share of the pressure drop that the wake accounts for
